utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning. The reason why we are starting late is well known to you already because we had a Status Conference in another case. Everyone is here except Mr. Bourgon, Mr. McCloskey. Yes. Mr. Ostojic was still in possession of the floor. He hadn't finished his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, to you, sir. We are proceeding with the cross-examinations today. I don't know quite whether we will finish, but -- yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, good morning. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If I may just try to get some estimate and perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- just provide some guidance with what we hope to accomplish today. I've polled my learned colleagues and I think there will be approximately two and a half to two and three-quarters hours of cross-examination still to go with this witness. So the first item is, I think we may be able to finish if we go to the usual closing time, plus maybe 20 minutes, as Your Honour had offered previously, in order to get this witness home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's see how we go, because again, for example, I mean Mr. Ostojic had required initially 45, but when he said that he needed more, we did not stop him. And likewise, we will treat the other Defence teams with this witness. So you never know exactly how. We will try.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We've lost three-quarters -- no. We've lost a session.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The second part is, Your Honour, we do have the next witness on deck, but given even the most optimistic estimates, I would request leave to release that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think you can safely send him to his hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So, Mr. Ostojic. Good morning to you, sir, as I said, we are continuing with the cross-examinations. If you can make an effort to finish by 2.45 -- by 1.45, I think we will appreciate that. Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Your Honour, I don't have any further questions I would like the opportunity to discuss with the Court in the absence of the witness, not today, but the difference between, obviously with all due respect to the Court, speculation and what reasonable inferences are and I'd like to come back to my questions because I have the similar-type questions with other witnesses and with the most respect to the Court I think there is a big difference when we discuss things that are speculative such as possible and those things that are reasonable inferences. But at this time, given the Court's statements yesterday I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to distinguish inferences made by you and inferences that you expect the witness to make and that's a basic difference. So who is next? Ms. Nikolic. You had indicated initially about 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you a few questions of a general nature with regard to the identification of the participants in conversations, the questions that have remained unanswered so far. Yesterday you spoke in great detail on page 67 of the transcript as well as on 21st November on page 56, you spoke about the moment when the participants in a conversation are identified. I'm trying to understand the principle. You explained in great detail -- based on Exhibit 1164, the Prosecutor's exhibit, you explained that when you reached a certain part in the conversation in which a person who had already introduced themselves and who had already been identified and when that person speaks to person X and the person who has agreed to the contents of the conversation, and based on who asked for that participant you tried to establish a link between the participants. I'm trying to be here clear; however, I wasn't clear on what you said that's why my proposal or my statement is so ambiguous. Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-132 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. All the time we are talking about the ways a -- participants can introduce themselves and there is a participant being introduced by somebody else. I don't know if there are any other such examples. However, those who monitored my work have accepted that such a way can be accepted and they had taken the material into account as being correct. And I'm going to tell you why and I'm going to explain the way we worked. First of all, we never knew what kinds of controls we had within our service, and those controls and checks could be carried out at any moment, at any place, and I never knew when and where, which means that it was always desirable and we always expected from somebody else to have the same document, and then we would make a puzzle of all these documents. We did that. And if something was found to be unacceptable and which could not be accepted then we had the rest of the material that could be built up on the material that we had.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown Exhibit P1161A in English, B, B/C/S version, and can we please go into private session because of a possibility that my next set of questions will reveal the witness's identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session. One moment, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there's been a translation problem. I have no objection if this document is admitted for a limited scope, but I have an objection if the document is for the content of the conversation contained in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is another matter. That is another matter. Let's look at the document itself. If there are no objections. Do I take it that this -- the registrar will proceed to admit -- to order the admitting of these documents? Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We would like to say that we will have a reservation with regarding the acceptability of all the intercepts in general terms. I only wish to remind you of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry. Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the list is concerned, I believe that the list contains the entire notebook number 9 with all the intercepts, if I'm not mistaken. They have not been translated into English save for those which are pertinent to this witness and some other witnesses that will accompany the testimony of each of the witnesses that are upcoming. In that sense, I don't see the relevance of the complete set of notebooks where intercepts were recorded, because for every witness and for every operative there will be intercepts in English to accompany their respective testimonies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. With respect to that point, it is our intention to offer the -- well, the translation of the relevant portion but, in addition, the physical notebook itself. As we've already seen, these witnesses are being shown these notebooks. They are leafing through them. There are pages and markings that have been identified throughout them, and out of an abundance of caution we would offer the actual physical notebook in addition to the translations of those relevance portions, those intercepts that have been in offer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But I think we need also to make our verifications particularly as to which of these documents need to be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So our suggestion is that we'll all take our time to go through this, also the Defence exhibits, and we'll revisit this first thing Monday morning when we resume, and we will finalise the process of tendering these documents on Monday. So I thank you. I wish to thank not only all of you for your cooperation but -- and in particular the -- all the staff for having been very, very understanding and very cooperative with us. Thank you so much. We'll all meet on Monday morning at 9.00 in this same courtroom. Thank you. Next week it will always be in the morning, and there will be no sitting on Friday, as you know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 27th day of November, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.19 p.m.,
